https://www.politico.eu/article/friedric.text: A conservative German mayor’s €10,000 donation to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is making things awkward for his party’s leaders. Bernd Prange, a Christian Democrat who serves as mayor of Altmärkische Höhe in Saxony-Anhalt, wrote in an open letter on Wednesday that he would be voting for the AfD in the state’s upcoming election on Sept. 6. “I want the AfD to become so strong in the Saxony-Anhalt election that it can govern alone,” wrote Prange. The goal, he said, was for his own party to “finally wake up,” tear down Germany’s political firewall and abandon what he called its shift to the left. Advertisement Advertisement The letter prompted swift criticism from within his own party: “I don’t like it. I can say that very clearly,” Saxony-Anhalt CDU Premier Sven Schulze told POLITICO’s Berlin Playbook Podcast on Thursday . “I think his approach is wrong. Definitely,” adding that he did not share Prange’s views “in any way.” As for whether the mayor will remain a Christian Democrat, Schulze was in no rush to make a call: “We’ll deal with the issue after the election,” he said. “Right now, it’s campaign time.” In an interview published earlier on Wednesday, Schulze had dismissed speculation about possible defections after the election: “No, someone switching from the CDU to the AfD will not happen,” he said. And while Prange hasn’t formally changed political allegiance, he said he wants Chancellor Friedrich Merz “removed” as CDU leader and accused him of running a party that is “giving up the conservative core of the Union.” The episode hits the CDU at a perilous moment, as Merz struggles to maintain the country’s “firewall” against cooperation with the far right while support for the AfD surges across eastern Germany. The AfD is polling between 41 and 43 percent in Saxony-Anhalt — almost twice the CDU’s 22 to 24 percent — putting the far right within striking distance of governing alone. Merz continues to rule out cooperation with the AfD, but September’s elections will put that under sustained pressure: Saxony-Anhalt votes on Sept. 6, followed by Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sept. 20. In an example close to home, her father Arthur Schneier’s historic Upper East Side synagogue was targeted by menacing anti-Israel protesters last year. The Holocaust-surviving 96-year-old, who founded the organization where Schneier Dresbach is executive vice president, told The Post last November that the protest l eft him shaken. “I don’t know how you expect a man to feel who saw his synagogue burn to the ground as a child and now has his synagogue attacked twice in the United States — and now to witness, almost on a daily basis, the egregious attacks, these heinous attacks on houses of worship, synagogues, [on Jews] … It’s insanity!” Schneier Dresbach said. 5 A rally against antisemitism near Central Synagogue in Manhattan on Aug. 19, 2026. James Messerschmidt for NY Post “The question is: When does it end and how does it end?” Her father, who still serves as the Appeals of Conscience Foundation’s president, fled Budapest and arrived in the United States in 1947. He founded the organization to promote religious freedom, human rights, peace and inter-religious dialogue across the globe and received the Presidential Citizens Medal from then-President Bill Clinton in 2001. Schneier Dresbach also referred to the recent “premeditated” alleged hate crime committed at Central Synagogue by wacko Larry Montes. The antisemite barged into the house of worship on Lexington Avenue and East 55th Street during a Shabbat service — and allegedly attacked a congregant and a security guard, unleashing chaos on the peaceful place. 5 Larry Montes (center) barged into Central Synagogue during a Shabbat service earlier this month. Central Synagogue “It’s very premeditated. When somebody says, ‘Oh, the guy who ran into Central Synagogue was a crazy person.’ He wasn’t so crazy,” Schneier Dresbach said. “If he was crazy, he would have gone out anywhere in the street and yelled. He specifically picked a synagogue.” Mamdani’s office had no immediate comment on Schneier Dresbach’s accusations. But the mayor has said he has “zero tolerance” for antisemitism or any kind of bigotry and has dedicated more funds to address it. “The Mamdani administration will continue using every tool at our disposal to stamp out hatred and build a city where every New Yorker is not only safe, but feels a true sense of inclusion and belonging,” a Mamdani spokesperson told The Post last week.
